events.title: The leader of PwC's 2,200-person DC office says clients expect some consulting work twice as fast as a year ago
events.summary: Jeanelle Johnson, managing partner of PwC in the Washington DC area PwC AI is raising clients' expectations for faster delivery times on consulting projects. Jeanelle Johnson, PwC's DC managing partner, said clients now expect some work to be delivered in half the time. Faster delivery should not be confused with less work, said Johnson. AI is resetting assumptions about how quickly professional services firms should move, and consulting clients are getting impatient. "I am seeing clients ask for our help in delivering outcomes at a more rapid pace" compared to this time last year, Jeanelle Johnson, PwC's managing partner for the Washington DC area, told Business Insider. "Something that we might have said takes eight to 10 weeks; the expectation is probably half of that. The shelf life is half," Johnson said. Clients are not necessarily expecting an entire transformation to be completed in a fraction of the time; the expectation is more for pilots and proofs of concepts, she said. "There's an expectation now that tools should accelerate the work," she added. Johnson leads more than 2,200 consulting and accounting employees in her role as PwC's DC managing partner. Asked whether those compressed timelines were putting pressure on her consulting teams, she said: "We're working on it." The Big Four professional services firms — PwC, Deloitte, KPMG, and EY — alongside firms like McKinsey, BCG, and Accenture, are at the center of the AI shift sweeping through workplaces. They have raced to build internal chatbots, train staff, and test AI in client work. The technology can now assist with, and increasingly perform, early-stage consulting tasks such as market research, due diligence, and brainstorming. At McKinsey, AI has accelerated the early problem-solving cycle, turning what used to be a team's "week one answer" — the first hypothesis after a week of research and analysis — into an "hour one answer," Kate Smaje, McKinsey's Global Leader for technology and AI, told Business Insider in June. That frees up consultants to spend more time testing deeper parts of the issue tree rather than waiting days to get oriented, Smaje said. Have a tip or story to share about working in consulting? Contact this reporter via email at pthompson@businessinsider.com or Signal at Polly_Thompson.89. Use a personal email address, a nonwork WiFi network, and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely . Amid the rank and file, employees at top firms have told Business Insider they're seeing a difference in delivery times due to AI. A software engineer at Deloitte US told Business Insider that some coding tasks had fallen from a dayslong process to around five minutes with AI, and an EY-Parthenon consultant in the UK said that due diligence that previously took two weeks of manual work and spreadsheet handling can now be completed in a day with AI. As well as pressure to deliver faster results, the shift is also raising questions about how the pricing model that has rested on human labor will adapt as more work gets done by AI. The work is more complex For Johnson, faster delivery should not be confused with less work. AI will change how consultants spend their time , freeing capacity for more meaningful or higher-value work rather than simply reducing the number of hours needed on a project, she told Business Insider. The work itself is also becoming more complex, she added. Clients are navigating geopolitical tensions, wars, tariffs, and macroeconomic uncertainty simultaneously — a broader set of pressures than consultants would often have helped them tackle in the past. "The confluence of all those things at the same time is something that we used to deal with one or two things at a time," Johnson said. "Now we're in a world order where we have to deal with 10 plus, plus, plus at a time." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: From BFFs to open war: Better.com’s founder vs. the investor who replaced him
events.summary: Hours after Better.com founder Vishal Garg was ousted as CEO this summer, the board member picked to replace him texted Garg after midnight. “You are the last person I am texting tonight—you are on my mind,” interim CEO Daniel Lewis wrote, according to a log of texts between the two reviewed by Fortune . “You are in my heart, whether you believe it or not.” The two men had a history of mutual affection, even if circumstances were now testing it. In April, Garg texted Lewis about becoming “BFFs” as the pair collaborated. At one point, it seemed like the engaged investor was just the boost Garg needed to help turn around the business he founded in 2014 to make getting a mortgage faster and cheaper online, and grow the flagship “Tinman” AI product for approving and closing home loans. Within weeks of the CEO change, however, the budding bromance was officially dead. Garg took Lewis to task in a group chat on X with Better.com investors, blasting the new CEO for working remotely in the South of France instead of the New York City office. Lewis hit back with a seven-part thread on X questioning his predecessor’s credibility and calling Garg a “bully.” Better’s board claims the company “accumulated more than $2 billion in net losses and lost more than 90% of its value as a public enterprise” under Garg’s tenure. Lewis ended the X thread with a line summing up his perspective on the relationship. “The love died when the diligence began,” Lewis wrote. Garg remains on the board for now, and he and his backers are fighting Lewis and the rest of the board for control over the $230 million company. The decision will come down to shareholders including Activant Capital, Framework Ventures, and SoftBank Capital Partners. Rarely does such a feud spill out into the open. But with control of the publicly traded company set to be decided by a shareholder vote—the contest deadline is Oct. 20—both men have taken their cases public, through dueling SEC filings, competing threads on X, and press releases . Fortune reviewed thousands of text messages exchanged between Garg and Lewis over 13 months that show how quickly the kinship between a founder and an investor who wanted to coach him pivoted into open hostility. For any founder who has taken outside money, or any investor who has gotten close to one, the Garg-Lewis rupture is a cautionary tale about how fast a partnership built on shared ambition can curdle—and how little a boardroom, or a friendship, can do to contain it once it does. Behind the curtain If the name Better sounds familiar, it’s probably thanks to the PR nightmare that followed when Garg, in December 2021 during the height of the COVID pandemic, laid off 900 employees on a Zoom call. Garg was accused of being insensitive and tone deaf about the job losses, which he blamed on a lack of productivity and a collapse in demand for refinancing. “I got some negative press for that,” said Garg, referring to the Zoom call. “But it also saved the company because the company was burning $100 million a month, right? We had too many people.” The losses didn’t stop after the 2021 layoffs but in recent years they have begun to recede. Better’s annual reports show net losses of $301 million that year, then $877.1 million in 2022, $536.4 million in 2023, $206.3 million in 2024, and $165.9 million in 2025. Revenue has also been on the rise, from $72.3 million in 2023 to $108.5 million in 2024, and $164.9 million in 2025.  In its annual reports for 2023 and 2024, Better disclosed a weakness in internal controls after an outside law firm’s review of the company’s culture found that “certain actions taken by our CEO failed to set a tone at the top that supported a strong culture of internal controls.” The 2024 report states Garg completed executive coaching “to address behavioral aspects of his management style to the satisfaction of the board of directors.” The tone-at-the-top weakness and others were remediated as of Dec. 31, 2025 and Garg noted that the SEC and Consumer Financial Protection Bureau investigated and “found nothing” against him or the company. Lewis, who founded investment firm Orange Capital 20 years ago, decided to invest in Better in 2025, becoming one of the largest outside shareholders (Lewis currently holds a stake between 2% and 3% in the company). From July 2025 to August 2026, Lewis and Garg exchanged at least 2,000 text messages, according to a log Garg shared with Fortune . The two compared notes about how to strengthen Better’s operations, and Lewis offered up investor relations advice to Garg. Eventually, their texts spilled over to their personal lives and families. Lewis invited Garg out to Nashville and got him to meet up with Lewis and his wife at the swanky sushi spot Nobu in downtown Manhattan. The two bonded over their shared passion for the minutiae of corporate finance and AI, humblebragging about ducking out of date nights and parties in favor of trying to “3x” in distressed debt trades.  “Birds of a feather,” Garg wrote to Lewis when he discovered they both made similar trades during the Great Financial Crisis. The two men came from different worlds but shared a love for finance. Garg, 48, grew up in Queens and went to public school, taking his first job at 14 making $6.50 an hour on a Wall Street trading desk, he said. He dropped out of traditional finance in 1998 to strike out on his own, starting an online student loan company, MyRichUncle.com, before he founded Better. Lewis, 51, is a die-hard Buffalo Bills fan who finished Cornell at 20 before moving to Tokyo to work for Citibank. He started on the Salomon Brothers trading floor in the 1990s, investing globally in special situations (unusual, one-time events that might be fatal for a business). He ran a hedge fund and later a family office, and spent five years running a Toronto software company. Both thrive on the grind. Last year during the holidays, Garg told Lewis to “have a tequila shot and just let it all go” while on vacation in Mexico. “My ability to relax is the same as yours,” wrote Lewis. “Doing my best.” In an October 2025 text to Lewis, Garg wrote “this time around” he is focusing on humility and gratitude, and that he printed the two words out “in big type and put up on my wall so I don’t forget.” Garg also texted Lewis about his CEO role, writing that he needed to run leadership for the direct-to-consumer division’s sales culture “in the kindest way, a boiler room sweat shop.” “My flaw was hiring and promoting same type of people. events.title: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario
events.summary: Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity When reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety and the fate of humanity, he said no. His argument: China . “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.” Trump was echoing a message the AI industry has put out for years. The US is in a heated technological race with China, companies including Anthropic and OpenAI have argued , and any regulation that would cede the contest risks incalculable economic and political harm. Even as Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, led an industry-wide call this week to “pace the frontier”, he declared that the US could only slow down to the point where China could not catch up. “If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” Amodei warned. The AI industry’s concerns about China may come with self-serving economic incentives, but they also reflect a strain of hawkish foreign policy toward Beijing that has become entrenched in tech. In recent years, parts of Silicon Valley have positioned themselves as the vanguard in a new cold war with China, arguing fiercely that the industry’s technological advancements are essential to both US hegemony and the liberal world order. This view has taken hold across tech’s different ideological camps, creating strange bedfellows of AI safety advocates, techno-militarists and neoconservatives, all of them fearful of Beijing. AI companies have hired former top US government staffers from both the Biden and Trump administrations to shape public strategy and analyze geopolitical risk, setting up in-house policy teams. Influential tech leaders have meanwhile written essays and policy documents calling for efforts to deter and degrade China’s AI capabilities, sometimes advocating for threatening armed conflict if necessary, in an attempt to influence foreign policy. As public calls for reining in the AI industry intensify and the risks associated with the technology increase, various industry forces are trying to ensure they are the ones with the answer to the question “what about China?”. Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this article. Few have been more vocal about the threat of Chinese state-controlled artificial intelligence than Amodei. The Anthropic CEO has argued for years that one of the reasons he’s so animated to advance AI is to ensure that the technology falls into the hands of Democratic governments and not oppressive regimes such as China. Amodei’s position has made him one of Silicon Valley’s most vocal critics of China’s tech industry, separating him from fellow AI leaders such as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman or Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, who frame the competition more in corporate or economic terms; and people such as Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, who have encouraged the use of Chinese AI models. Demis Hassabis, the leader of Google Deepmind, has made few public remarks on China in comparison with his peers. “Sam Altman doesn’t have especially strong views when it comes to China. Anthropic is a totally different story,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Amodei is really, really focused on a particular view of the risk from AI and what he frames as basically a struggle between a world dominated by authoritarian AI versus democratic AI”. Amodei’s argument, which he has laid out over a series of essays, is that China acquiring superpowered AI is one of the most severe threats posed by the technology. He believes humanity is approaching the creation of an ultra-advanced AI, and that such a tool would give an authoritarian state the ability to create a “swarm of millions or billions of fully automated armed drones” that would be “capable of both defeating any military in the world and suppressing dissent within a country by following around every citizen”. “There are a number of possible arguments against the severity of these threats, and I wish I believed them, because AI-enabled authoritarianism terrifies me,” Amodei wrote in January in an essay called The Adolescence of Technology. Amodei has long asserted that in order to stop China’s advancement, the US and its allies should take aggressive action to limit Chinese AI companies’ growth – most notably blocking the sale of advanced semiconductor chips and manufacturing equipment necessary for improving AI. (Huang of Nvidia has bristled at this position, calling export controls a failure and urging Trump to ease restrictions.

events.title: Domestic datacentres: how computer power can help heat your home
events.summary: Energy bills are scheduled to rise next month but there are innovative ways to heat your home and save money ‘When Giles Gibson turns on the hot tap in his home, the water that comes out of it is not heated by gas but by the tiny datacentre strapped to the tank. Attached to the hot water cylinder in his London home is a compact computer server that generates heat and then transfers it as it operates. Gibson gets the benefit of hot water when he needs it at a reduced cost, while the heat that is generated by the server is not lost into the air, a big environmental problem with large datacentres around the world. “As soon as I read about it, I thought: ‘This is obvious – why wouldn’t you do this?’”he says. “It just makes sense to take a computer out of a datacentre and to strap it next to your water tank and get free heat.” Gibson estimates that the hot water bills for his four-bedroom house in south-east London have fallen by between £10 and £15 a month since he had the system installed last year. “So over a year, it adds up, and it’s just another little extra that helps,” Gibson says. “Having one of these units is a no-brainer.” With domestic energy bills set to rise again next month , and growing disquiet about the impact of large-scale datacentres on the environment, there are lots of projects looking at how to harness the heat being thrown out by computers. Gibson’s system, supplied by the Surrey-based company heata , is one of a number of innovative ideas on the market that aim to tackle the problem of waste heat on a domestic scale. Heata operates a sustainable cloud computing business that sends processing jobs from its clients to the servers in people’s homes. The devices have the combined power of about eight laptops. “What the home gives us is effectively somewhere to put a server that has a power connection, and a fibre connection, and a place for heat to go,” says Charlie Beharrell, commercial director of heata. He says the company aims to provide about 80% of the heat needed for a home’s hot water. “The water in their hot water cylinder will effectively be heated by our server, and they might have to use the gas boiler for the peakier moments in the day, like when they have a bath,” Beharrell says. “The idea is that the primary heating system is working a lot less hard to heat the water than it would normally have to do if our system wasn’t in place.” It can only work in homes with vented, unpressurised water cylinders, typically recognisable by the blue insulation around the outside. A container with the server in is attached to the front of the cylinder after engineers cut a hole in the insulation. It is glued to the boiler with a thermal paste so the unit can conduct heat to the cylinder with no plumbing involved. There is no cost for the installation. “It takes a couple of hours and we retrofit it to the domestic water system,” Beharrell says. Heata pays for the electricity that is used to keep the server running, while the homeowner pays for the fibre broadband connection that is necessary. Beharrell says that millions of homes are fitted with vented water cylinders, while the units can also work with heat pumps. However, the system is not suitable for homes with combi boilers. A version for unvented cylinders is in development. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Heata’s units are now in 100 homes and there are 3,000 people on the waiting list for installation. Anyone interested in having one can sign up on the company’s website, heata.co. The company says hundreds more are expected to be installed next year. In a separate project in Essex , two households are testing a concept where almost 500 matchbox-sized computers are stored together to form a mini datacentre, and the heat generated from them is converted into energy. The freezer-sized HeatHub units are made by the Wales-based company thermify and, like heata’s, also recycle the energy created when computers process tasks. They work differently from the heata system and the makers say they could one day replace domestic boilers. The heat created by the rows of Raspberry Pi computers warms a mineral oil that surrounds them. “The computers get the mineral oil hot,” says thermify’s chief executive, Travis Theune. “We send that through a heat exchanger. The heat exchanger heats up the water that’s going through a radiator, and the radiator delivers heat to the room. It’s the same basic concept as an induction heater.” The existing units have 480 computers in them, which carry out tasks for companies that buy time to process the work they want done. Theune says that the company plans to make a range of units to cater for different-sized homes. For example, a three- to four-bedroom house will have a unit which is about the size of a washing machine, while a flat could have one the size of a microwave.

events.title: Inside the squishy nightmare: Explosions, burns, and thousands of calls to poison control
events.summary: Jim Franco/Albany Times Union via Getty Images; Rebecca Zisser/BI Warning: Some of the images you may see are graphic. For questions or if you suspect a poisoning, contact Poison Help at PoisonHelp.org or call 1-800-222-1222. Katie Zerbst was doing laundry on a Sunday morning in June when she heard a "guttural" moan. "It was the sound that makes you just drop everything and run," the 45-year-old mother told Business Insider. Rushing into the kitchen, Zerbst found her 10-year-old daughter, Violet, covered in steaming hot, sparkly goo. Burns seared across her face, and skin from her top lip was flapping down into her mouth. Moments earlier, Violet had popped a squishy toy into the microwave for 30 seconds. She wanted to make the glittery cube more malleable so she could squish it more easily. When she pulled it out, it erupted like a volcano. Violet ended up in the emergency room, and she isn't the only child to visit the hospital after playing with a squishy. Violet Zerbst, 10, suffered burns on her face and body after a squishy toy exploded. Katie Zerbst Business Insider reviewed dozens of incident reports, spoke to parents, and consulted doctors and regulators about the risks behind this year's biggest toy craze. Despite a spike in reports of burns and concerns about toxic exposure, oversight of squishies — slime-filled toys shaped like dumplings, fruit, ice cubes, and other cute characters — falls into a regulatory gray area, and the market is teeming with counterfeits and knockoffs. Have a squishy story to share? Reach out to Business Insider correspondent Jane Ridley: jridley@businessinsider.com. What's in a squishy? Squishies, with their gooey, foamy, or gel-like textures, fall into the category of "sensory toys," like fidget spinners, kinetic sand, and magnetic balls. In recent years, the toys have gone "from zero to hero," Five Below CEO Winnie Park told investors in June. They're helping the retailer to become "America's greatest little toy store" by driving brick-and-mortar traffic, Park said on September's earnings call. Kohl's also credited the toy with a sales bump, and workers from several retailers have taken to social media with tales of over-eager customers demanding their favorite squishies. Instagram and TikTok are full of satisfying videos of hands squishing toys shaped like a strawberry or a tube of toothpaste. However, reports from homes and hospitals across the country describe exploding and leaking toys, along with chemical smells. America's Poison Centers told Business Insider that more than half of the 11,500 reports about squishies received by its member organizations since 2024 happened in the first six months of 2026, though only a small portion of the ruptures caused severe injury. Schylling, which manufactures the most popular squishy brand, NeeDoh, was hit with two lawsuits in July over squishy explosions that plaintiffs say resulted in severe burns. One complaint said that a NeeDoh Nice Cube, left lying on a TV stand near a window, remained cool to the touch but, when squeezed, erupted with a scalding gel that left blisters on the person's leg. Lawyers for the company declined to comment on the allegations. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission has also seen a spike in squishy-related incident reports from shoppers and hospitals this year. A Business Insider review found about two dozen consumers describing how ruptures — due to microwaves, hot cars, and squeezing — have burned kids this year. Roughly 20 more reported strong smells emanating from the squishy toys . Hospital reports collected by CPSC showed about a dozen explosion cases in 2025, the latest year available. One parent told the CPSC the toy didn't "just pop"; it "exploded" in February 2024 after their daughter squeezed it on her 10th birthday. This August, another reported that their 8-year-old son was squeezing his squishy normally when it ruptured. "The outer layer of the toy failed without warning, spraying the internal filling directly across my son's face and into his eyes," causing immediate "burning and distress," the report said. A February report to CPSC echoed a common complaint about a squishy that "emitted an extremely powerful and persistent chemical odor, resembling acetone or nail polish remover," which gave its owner a headache. In response to growing public concern, the CPSC issued guidance in August, warning shoppers of serious burn hazards from intentionally or unintentionally exposing toys to heat. A spokesperson told Business Insider that these toys hit on several longstanding concerns for the agency, including the dangers of water beads and potential exposure to unsafe chemicals. As for the dangers of microwaving them? That's considered improper use, and the agency doesn't typically punish companies when consumers don't follow safety warnings, the spokesperson said. Underlying these reports is the common frustration that squishy ingredients vary widely and often aren't listed on the packaging. NeeDoh discloses that its products, including the Nice Cube, Dream Drop, and Groovy Glob, use fairly common ingredients such as maltose sugar, cornstarch, and polyvinyl alcohol, the latter of which the brand says is non-toxic and also found in white glue. While these ingredients are considered chemically safe, the lawsuit in California cites academic research to argue that some of these substances have thermal properties that, along with a soft polymer casing, can make scalding hot gel feel deceptively cool to the touch — until the toy pops. The market is also rife with knock-offs, and federal safety rules are patchy. US regulations don't require independent testing and certification of toys, unless they're marketed to children under 13. Manufacturers initially decide how to market and age-grade their products, subject to CPSC oversight. While products clearly intended for young children, such as baby pacifiers or toddler teethers, must meet stricter testing requirements, squishies can plausibly be sold as children's toys, adult stress balls, desk accessories, or collectibles. Many are marketed as products for all ages, and verifying a toy's age classification can involve a lengthy review. That ambiguity raises a broader question: When an all-ages product becomes wildly popular with children, should it be treated as a children's toy ? The CPSC says it considers not just a product's label, but also how it's designed, marketed, and reasonably understood and used by consumers when determining whether it's a children's product. That last part can change over time, and sometimes it shifts faster than regulators can keep up with. The agency said that reputable brands typically go beyond legal requirements by seeking voluntary safety certification from independent organizations, such as ASTM International or United Laboratories, and include their logos on their packaging. An ASTM spokesperson told Business Insider the organization's standards are periodically review

events.title: ‘A huge problem’: Trump has traded more stocks than all of Congress combined. A Bush-era ethics lawyer explains why you should worry
events.summary: President Donald Trump has made more securities trades since returning to office than every member of Congress combined. According to a Bloomberg analysis published this week, he has made roughly 28,700 in 17 months, or about 80 trades every market day, It’s a new habit of Trump’s. In his first term, Trump’s financial disclosures consisted mostly of his real estate and privately held businesses.  For his second term, the periodic reports he filed through early 2026 showed an account buying municipal and corporate bonds—more than $100 million by August 2025 and more than $337 million in all—along with bank preferred securities and bond ETFs. The stock trading surfaced in May of this year, when a first-quarter filing listed roughly 3,600 transactions in 90 days. Then the annual disclosure, released June 30 at nearly a thousand pages, showed more than 21,000 trades in 2025, worth between $600 million and $1.86 billion, at 85 per market day. Trump lists eight separate investment accounts but doesn’t give any indication of which institutions manage them. “I believe that that is a huge problem,” Richard Painter, who served as chief White House ethics lawyer under President George W. Bush and now teaches securities law at the University of Minnesota, told Fortune . “I’ve gone through every president. I don’t think we’ve had any president trade in the stock market.” Since Lyndon Johnson, essentially every president has used a blind trust, held index funds, or just owned Treasuries. Jimmy Carter, for example, put the family peanut business in a blind trust that eventually sold it. However, Trump’s portfolio is handled differently. In May, after the stock trades appeared, White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Fortune the assets are held in a trust managed by the president’s children. Eric Trump posted that any suggestion a family member was buying individual stocks “would be a lie and blatantly false.”  “There’s a financial conflict of interest if he has an ownership interest in the account,” Painter said. “It doesn’t matter who manages it.” In a statement, the White House’s Ingle told Fortune that third-party financial institutions independently manage the portfolio through “computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000.” He did not answer questions about which institutions manage the portfolio or why the White House described a family trust in May. “There are no conflicts of interest,” the statement said. Fortune’s review of the president’s first-quarter filing in May found the account bought up to $1.38 million of DoorDash stock; in April, Trump had DoorDash deliver a McDonald’s order to the White House for a tipped-worker tax event. The account sold hyperscaler stocks in the $5 million-$25 million range on Feb. 10, the day after a chip-tariff carveout leaked. It bought energy stocks in the weeks after the Iran war began, as Trump was downplaying the conflict as a short-term conflagration. It bought Cal-Maine, the country’s largest egg producer, during the egg shortage and sold it two months later for two to five times more. Every executive branch official except the president and vice president has to abide by 18 U.S.C. 208, a criminal statute that bars participation in government matters that affect one’s own holdings. “If he were Treasury Secretary, he’d have a big, big problem with that account,” Painter said. He was careful, though, not to allege that anyone is trading on government information, which could constitute criminal insider trading, explaining that stock-trading disclosures can’t prove that. That, Painter said, is the argument for a ban. A new House measure, passed in July and attached to a voter-ID bill, bars members, spouses and dependent children from trading stocks; Trump endorsed it in his State of the Union address, saying it should pass “without delay” so Congress “cannot corruptly profit from using insider information.” Yet when Sen. Josh Hawley advanced a version last July that would have extended the ban to the president and vice president—not until 2029, after Trump leaves office—Trump called him a “pawn” playing “right into the dirty hands of the Democrats,” and a “second-tier Senator.” To Painter, this is all familiar. On Jan. 6, 2021—”obviously, there was some other news that day,” he added—he and Indiana University law professor Donna Nagy published a letter to congressional leadership calling for a ban on stock trading by members, the president and the vice president. Neither party acted on it; Republicans wanted to avoid embarrassing Trump, while Democrats wanted to avoid embarrassing Nancy Pelosi, whose husband is an active trader. The stakes are pretty clear to Painter. “If the president owns a bunch of oil company stocks, he’s making money if the price of oil goes up,” he said. “So if he bombs Iran and the price of oil goes up and he owns oil company stocks, he’s making money, and the rest of us are paying for  $6 gas.” The account bought energy stocks in March. “If it’s like a mutual fund,” Painter said, “why not just buy a mutual fund?” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Warren Buffett has stepped down as Berkshire chairman. Here are 5 leadership lessons he leaves behind.
events.summary: Warren Buffett's decades leading Berkshire Hathaway yielded numerous lessons, including learning from mistakes. Nati Harnik/AP This week, the Oracle of Omaha gave up his job of chairman of Berkshire Hathaway. After decades at the top, Warren Buffett leaves a legacy of leadership advice. He has emphasized the importance of self-improvement, honesty, and choosing the right leaders. If you want to be a high-mileage leader like Warren Buffett, it pays to be humble. The Oracle of Omaha this week gave up the job as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, after more than half a century spent building and then running the conglomerate. Buffett said his son Howard would succeed him as chairman. In that role, his son will guard Berkshire's culture and values, which the elder Buffett said are "worth more than anything on our balance sheet." That belief in the importance of organizational culture is nothing new for Buffett who has, over the years, offered a steady stream of advice on investing and leadership. Last year, in his final Thanksgiving letter to shareholders as CEO, he shared insights on the virtues of stewardship, honesty, and what he described as "good intentions" gone awry in attempts to rein in CEO pay. One broad takeaway was his call to continue learning and growing. "Choose your heroes very carefully and then emulate them. You will never be perfect, but you can always be better," Buffett wrote. Here are five other lessons Buffett shared: Stay humble The 96-year-old famously ran Berkshire with an unfussy, meat-and-potatoes sensibility. Buffett wrote about the role luck played in his life and work, and how that experience continually honed his sense of humility. "Keep in mind that the cleaning lady is as much a human being as the Chairman," Buffett said. He also grounded some of his humble inclinations in the luck he had, being a man — compared with his sisters, whom he described as having "equal intelligence and better personalities," though they faced a much different outlook. "I was born in 1930 healthy, reasonably intelligent, white, male and in America. Wow! Thank you, Lady Luck," he said. Learn from your errors Buffett said that while he's made many mistakes, he's tried to use them as springboards for growth. "Learn at least a little from them and move on," Buffett wrote. One misstep, he said, was not intervening more forcefully when he saw indications that a "wonderful and loyal CEO" of a parent or subsidiary company would "succumb to dementia, Alzheimer's or another debilitating and long-term disease." "Charlie and I encountered this problem several times and failed to act. This failure can be a huge mistake," Buffett wrote, referring to Charlie Munger, his longtime friend and colleague, who died in 2023. Buffett said that while it's often not easy, boards need to keep watch for signs of such conditions in chiefs, and that CEOs themselves need to do the same at the units they oversee. "Directors should be alert and speak up is all that I can advise," Buffett said in the letter, which ran about seven pages. Choose the right leaders Part of Buffett's call for humility extended to how future Berkshire leaders should expect to conduct themselves — and what they should aspire to. He said that the company should only require five or six CEOs over the next century. In the shareholder letter released Friday, Buffett reiterated his confidence in Greg Abel, who succeeded him as CEO. "He has been making the decisions that matter for some time now, and I have not had to think twice about any of them," Buffett wrote. Buffett wrote last fall that he wanted Berkshire Hathaway, which was a New England textile producer when he began buying up its stock in the early 1960s, to avoid hiring top leaders who are there for the wrong reasons: "It should particularly avoid those whose goal is to retire at 65, to become look-at-me rich or to initiate a dynasty," Buffett said of the company. Think about your obit One recurring theme in his letter centered on Buffett's assertion that it's "never too late to improve." Another bit of advice: Work backward from what you want your obituary to say and then "live the life to deserve it." The release of Buffett's third annual Thanksgiving letter to Berkshire shareholders had become something of an event because of his status as one of the world's most famous investors. He said at the time that he planned to continue to address shareholders in an annual letter , though not as CEO. "As the British would say, I'm 'going quiet.' Sort of." Don't rule from the grave Buffett's decision to become chairman emeritus appeared in line with his advice against of trying to retain influence for too long. In his Thanksgiving letter, Buffett applauded the abilities of Abel , who is some three decades younger and took over as CEO at the start of 2026. "He is a great manager, a tireless worker and an honest communicator," Buffett said. He also wrote about his three children, whom he said possess the "maturity, brains, energy and instincts" to disburse the family's large fortune . Earlier this year, Buffett's net worth was nearing $150 billion. After he dies, Buffett wrote last year, his children will be free to adapt to changes in tax policy and other factors as needed to continue the family's philanthropic work. "Ruling from the grave does not have a great record, and I have never had an urge to do so," he said. An earlier version of this story appeared on November 10, 2025. events.title: Trump says US has ‘permanent control’ of Greenland security: Does it?
events.summary: New agreement with Denmark falls short of Trump’s previously stated goal of US ‘ownership’ of the island. United States President Donald Trump claims the US has reached a deal with Denmark granting it “permanent control” over Greenland’s security “and all other needs”. The announcement comes more than a year after the US president threatened to seize the self-governing Arctic territory, which is part of Denmark. Those threats roiled the NATO security alliance that Washington and Copenhagen are part of. list 1 of 3 EU pledges more than $200m to Greenland amid Trump annexation threats list 2 of 3 US announces $400m investment in Australian rare earth mine list 3 of 3 Massive iceberg capsizes off the coast of Greenland According to Denmark, the deal is expected to be signed during next week’s United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York. Copenhagen has stressed that it retains sovereignty over Greenland, and this deal will still need to be ratified in the Danish and Greenland parliaments. Here’s what we know about the deal and what it could mean for the US and Greenland: The official text has yet to be released. But according to Trump, the deal gives the US permanent control over Greenland’s security and “all other needs”, at no cost to the US. The deal bars US adversaries from establishing a military presence or making “sensitive investments” in Greenland without US approval, said Trump. A US Department of State official cited by the BBC said the deal will mean non-NATO states won’t be able to set up bases in Greenland and will be barred from “making investments in Greenland that could threaten the United States”. The official said that means China and Russia won’t be able to build bases or send troops to Greenland, and that those states would be blocked from investing “in sensitive sectors”. However, Mikkel Olesen, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, told Al Jazeera that it is unlikely to be a major concession because “the Danes and Greenlanders never wished for Russia or China to have bases in Greenland.” However, it is unclear whether other countries could similarly be labelled “adversaries” to the US in the future, subjecting them to these restrictions. Trump called the deal an “‘Infinite Life’ Agreement”, meaning “it never ends”. The State Department official also said the agreement gives the US the right to build more military sites on the island without Greenland or Denmark approving. According to the official, the deal would remain in force even if Greenland were to become an independent state in the future. There was no specific mention of potential US mining rights in Greenland, which has a rich deposit of rare-earth minerals , including zinc, iron, uranium and graphite, that are likely to interest Trump. These minerals are highly sought after and are used in the manufacture of hundreds of technological products, from smartphones to fighter jets. However, some observers think this could be what Trump means by his mention of “sensitive investments”. The US president has sought to expand the US’s global access to rare-earth metals, especially as China, a global leader in the technology, AI and renewables industries with 60 percent of the world’s known deposits of these minerals in its territory, restricts their exports . What have Greenland and Denmark said? Greenland and Denmark acknowledged the deal on Friday, but neither gave specific details about its terms. They said the agreement would be announced next week. Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it “recognises Greenland’s interests” and is “to the benefit of us all”. Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said it is “great for NATO and Europe”, as it “strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic Area”. Olesen stressed that details of the deal remain unclear and that available information should be taken “with a grain of salt” as most of it has so far come from the US side. Does the deal give the US ownership of Greenland? No, it does not meet Trump’s previously stated objective of “ownership”. Denmark’s Frederiksen said the agreement “recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination”. Olesen said the deal could be positive for Greenland and Denmark as it “has the potential to end the crisis” caused by Trump’s insistence on acquiring Greenland last year, without sacrificing sovereignty. Trump’s earlier threats to seize control of Greenland were met with high resistance on the island of 56,000 people. A January 2025 poll found that 85 percent of Greenlanders opposed becoming part of the US. What military rights does the US already have in Greenland? A substantial number. Under a 1951 treaty, the US has broad overflight and basing rights on the island.

events.title: Microsoft’s AI CEO says ‘controlling’ AI ‘is going to be a really, really big challenge’
events.summary: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman Bloomberg/Getty Images Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman said AI labs need to ensure they can control what they're creating. "We should not create something that we can't control," Suleyman said. Suleyman questioned why some in tech are so opposed to new regulations. Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman says it's "surreal" that he has to say AI needs to align with humanity. "We should not create something that we can't control," Suleyman said Friday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "And if it looks like we're on a path to producing something that is not just more powerful than all of us combined, but is, as a result, something that we can't control, then it's going to fail in its fundamental purpose." Success will not come easily, Suleyman said. "Controlling these things are going to be a really, really big challenge for us," he said. Suleyman said he was "glad to see a lot more people" supporting the idea that tech companies and frontier model makers need to maintain control over their AI systems. In the industry, ensuring AI acts in accordance with human intentions is called alignment. "But there's a growing group of people that think that we are doing it for its own sake, and we just want to turn over the next card, see what's around the corner, and create something that is just going to slip our own leash," he said. Suleyman's comments come at a time of increased attention to AI safety, after former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warned that AI workers are privately fearful that AI could wipe out humanity. In recent days, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have all expressed broad agreement that frontier AI labs should better pace their advancements to ensure that safety measures can keep up. Before Coxon's viral post, many in the industry were already concerned about safety after OpenAI revealed that its agents had breached Hugging Face , illustrating the potential consequences of losing control over AI systems. Suleyman called the breadth of the Hugging Face breach and OpenAI's initial unawareness of what its AI agents were doing "remarkable." "It has moved everybody from Elon and Zuck to me, Sam, Dario, and everybody else in between to say it's time that we take a look at this," Suleyman said. "I don't think it's overly alarmist. I don't think it's self-interested. I actually think it's responsible." Meta CEO Zuckerberg has taken a different stance than Amodei and other AI leaders. Earlier this week, Zuckerberg questioned why AI companies need to band together to manage the rate of development, suggesting that each company should handle its own business. "Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely," Zuckerberg wrote on X. Some in tech, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , have questioned whether broad new regulations are needed. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have also pushed back on AI companies that are urging governments to act. Amodei and others have requested Congress and international bodies to get involved as well. Suleyman questioned those who scoff at the very idea of regulation. "Regulation is not a nasty, dangerous word," he said. "Everything that you trust and is of value at the moment has been carefully thought through by standards bodies that involve the industry, the public, consumer protection, Congress. And we're just going through that process." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Africa’s Green Revolution threatens traditional foods
events.summary: The promotion of monocultures is hurting the production of much more nutritious and climate-resistant traditional crops. This year, AGRA, the donor-funded agricultural development initiative formerly known as the Alliance for a Green Revolution in Africa, is celebrating its 20th anniversary. AGRA’s slogan is “sustainably growing Africa’s food systems”, but for years, researchers and farmers have warned that the policies it promotes are having a negative impact on African agriculture. Our new research provides more evidence to that effect. We have documented how AGRA’s Green Revolution, with its well-funded promotion of commercial seeds, fertilisers and other inputs, has failed to spur the “productivity revolution” promised by its founders. Worse still, its promotion of monocultures, such as maize, has led to the massive expansion of land dedicated to them. At the same time, more resilient and nutritious local crops, such as millet, are losing ground. Funding the loss of traditional crops Hunger continues to increase in Africa, driven by climate change, desertification, conflict and disruptions to international supply lines from international conflicts like the Ukraine war. The Green Revolution promoted by AGRA does not seem to have made much of a difference. In countries where AGRA has had significant presence, the number of undernourished people has increased by about 60 percent – roughly the same rate as the rest of the continent. The United Nations is calling for greater attention to “affordable healthy diets”. For Africa’s small-scale farmers, who grow what their families and communities eat, that means more, not less, crop diversity, which is the opposite of what the Green Revolution has produced. In countries that have participated in AGRA projects, crops such as maize are promoted and funded with billions of dollars in subsidies and investment. Despite that, yields for maize have grown only modestly, just 40 percent over 18 years, well below the 100 percent improvement promised by AGRA. Some countries, like Malawi and Ethiopia, have seen stronger yield growth for maize, but some, such as Kenya – where AGRA’s headquarters are located – have seen yields decline. Maize production has soared across participant countries, driven mainly by the massive expansion of plantings as subsidies drive farmers to plant maize on new land. In contrast, our research shows that traditional African staples such as sorghum, cassava, and groundnuts have lost land and investment. Since AGRA was launched in 2006, 13 countries that have participated have seen a decline in productivity of 21 percent for cassava and 10 percent for groundnuts in total. But millet – a climate-resilient, nutritious grain – is the crop that has suffered the most. Before 2006, millet was as prevalent as maize in these countries. Since 2006, millet production has fallen 27 percent, while maize production has more than doubled. Millet yields have fallen 17 percent with the lack of investment. And as land allocated to maize production increased 71 percent, land for millet fell 12 percent. Millet is not some backward crop waiting to be replaced by maize. For generations, it has fed communities across some of Africa’s driest regions. It can withstand heat and drought, grow with relatively few external inputs, and provide nutritious food where other crops struggle. In 2023, the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) celebrated the “Year of Millets”, highlighting the multiple benefits of the crop to the environment and social welfare. The same is true of many of Africa’s traditional crops – sorghum, fonio, cowpeas, cassava, indigenous vegetables and many others. They are part of the biological diversity of African farming, but also of our cuisines, knowledge and cultures. At a time of climate change, pushing such crops aside makes particularly little sense. Farmers need more options in their fields, not fewer. A diverse farm spreads risk: when one crop suffers from drought, pests or disease, another may survive. Rotation and diversity of crops help keep soils more fertile. Rhetorically, AGRA now professes to value the very crops that its Green Revolution helped push to the margins. It speaks of diverse, nutritious and climate-adapted crops, and its seed programmes include millet, sorghum, cowpea, groundnut and others. We welcome serious investment in these crops. It is overdue. But there is no indication that AGRA and other Green Revolution proponents will abandon their chosen monocrops, such as maize. AGRA’s current seed strategy still emphasises improved varieties, certified seeds, faster variety turnover, commercialisation and market-oriented seed systems. Investment needs to support farmers’ rights to save, use, exchange and develop their seeds, protect crop diversity and indigenous knowledge, and ensure that farmers and communities – not seed markets alone – determine which varieties survive and spread.

events.title: Older Americans are sliding into poverty
events.summary: The supplemental poverty rate for older Americans has increased. Willowpix/Getty Images After a surge of pandemic-era aid, older Americans have faced rising poverty. Healthcare costs drive older Americans into poverty, straining their savings and finances. Social Security often isn't enough to cover costs, leading older Americans to take on low-paying jobs. After a slew of pandemic-induced aid ran its course, older Americans are falling back into poverty — and even younger would-be retirees are struggling. After the Great Recession, the trendline for older Americans had been improving, and 2020 pandemic relief measures helped buttress the aging population from falling into poverty in the wake of Covid. New census data shows that now, the poverty rate has increased the most for Americans 65 and older, after adjusting for things like tax credits and government programs. The share of all Americans living below that adjusted poverty measure grew from 9.1% in 2020 to 13.1% in 2025. For Americans 65 and older, that rate grew from 9.4% to 15.4%. Millions of older Americans live solely off Social Security benefits , which often don't cover all daily costs , let alone Medicare premiums or caregiving expenses. Social Security kept 28.8 million Americans out of poverty in 2025, the new Census report found, including nearly 21 million Americans 65 and older. As the boomer generation ages into retirement, those benefits look shaky, a worrying sign as lifespans stretch longer. Historically, poverty among older Americans rises with age, although younger retirement-aged Americans started falling into harder times as of 2024. Last year, Business Insider spoke with dozens of Americans 80 and older who were below or slightly above the poverty line, most of whom worked at least part time to make ends meet. Many said the only jobs they could find were minimum wage, menial jobs, paying them enough to put food on the table and heat their homes. Some said they had much more saved earlier in life, but were hit hard by medical treatments. "We should get tax breaks after a certain age because prices are so high for food," said Rebecca Reed, 88, who works two lower-paying jobs in New Orleans. "And maybe some discounts at the grocery store." Rebecca Reed works two part-time jobs at 88. Annie Flanagan for BI While the oldest Americans are still the most impoverished group, their younger counterparts have been seeing poverty rates tick up. The official poverty rate for Americans ages 70 to 74 saw the largest percentage-point increase from 2020 to 2024, according to a Business Insider analysis of Census microdata, followed by the younger cohort of 65- to 69-year-olds, indicating a more widely felt poverty landscape. Older Americans are often more prone to sudden and costly medical disruptions , which contribute to malnutrition or poor living conditions. Indeed, 7.7 million Americans fell into poverty due to medical expenses, per the Census report, and around 2.5 million of them were 65 and older. That's up from around 2.36 million in 2024. In interviews, dozens of families said they have spent six figures on care for their loved ones, as the median cost of a private nursing home room rose from $111,000 to $130,000 annually between 2022 and 2025, according to data from the care navigation platform CareScout. Some families said their older loved ones had exhausted all of their savings on home health aides or assisted living facilities, leaving them in the hands of their financially pressed children. Housing costs have also hurt many older Americans who don't own homes, or who have substantial home repairs. More than one in three older American households puts 30% or more of their income toward housing, per a 2025 study from Harvard University's Joint Center for Housing Studies . Older Americans are also the fastest-growing demographic experiencing homelessness, with about 20% of all people experiencing homelessness 55 and older as of 2024. Some are doing what they can to make the most of it. Sharon Albrecht, 85, works for a home healthcare agency and as a part-time Uber driver in Virginia to make ends meet. Though above the poverty line, Albrecht said her income goes a long way toward supplementing Social Security and her retirement savings, adding that she's "very wealthy in time and freedom to create my own schedule." "If an 80+ person has the attitude that 'Now, I have time to create,' the sky is the limit," Albrecht said. "It totally depends on the person and whether or not they have a victim mentality." events.title: I've spoken to my daughter in a non-native language since she was a baby. Now she corrects my French.
events.summary: The author has been speaking French to her daughter since she was a baby, even though it is not her native language. Courtesy of Tara McAllister. I hoped a bilingual upbringing would give my daughter an edge in life. I didn't realize that a non-native language to me would end up becoming our primary language. I've had my share of criticism over this decision, but it's working well for us so far. My daughter was born three months before the COVID-19 restrictions began where we live. Stuck at home with a new baby, I needed something to keep me busy, and I'm too mishap-prone for sourdough. For a linguist like me, a language-related project seemed like just the thing. I decided to dust off my French — which I spoke quite well in high school but hadn't used in decades — so I could speak it at home with my daughter. What parent hasn't heard about the benefits of bilingualism for little brains? Six years later, my project has outstripped all my expectations. We're lucky to have bilingual schools in our neighborhood. Because my daughter hears French from her peers as well as from me, she speaks it just as fluently as the English she uses with my husband and the rest of our family. My own ability to express myself in French grew little by little alongside hers. Today, we rarely speak English when it's just the two of us. Some people think I'm making a mistake My French is far from perfect: I'm never going to get rid of my American accent , and my speech is peppered with small mistakes — like le vidéo when it should be la vidéo . Sharing my family's language journey online, I've gotten criticism that my grammatical slips could harm my daughter's linguistic development. "If I wasn't fluent enough to not make errors, I would not be speaking that language to my child 100% of the time," one poster told me. Others have raised concerns about my emotional connection with my child. "The optimal language of interaction is the caregiver's heart language (most dominant language)," a commenter on a bilingual-parenting blog warned. The author said her daughter, now 6, often corrects her pronunciation. Courtesy of Tara McAllister. What the research shows Since I'm a linguist by profession, I did a deep dive into the literature on bilingual development at the start of my project, and what I learned reinforced my decision to focus on French. Many people believe that children are little sponges for language, but that's only half true. Children automatically soak up the language they hear in the surrounding community, especially from peers. But a language children hear mostly at home needs more encouragement to take root. And even if they don't absorb the whole language overnight, children do have an advantage in certain aspects of language learning. My daughter doesn't imitate my accent and my grammatical errors. Instead, she corrects them. "Le vidéo doesn't make any sense, maman," she once told me in French. The shared learning experience is invaluable I once asked my husband if he thought speaking French was damaging my emotional connection with our daughter, who is now 6 years old. He snorted. "If anything, you have the opposite problem. You two are weirdly close," he told me. It's true we have a very strong bond, what the French call une relation fusionnelle. And I suspect that our shared language journey has fostered that close connection rather than harming it. Learning French is a project my daughter and I have shared for six years. Our current dynamic is unique: I still have a larger vocabulary and can teach her new words, but she is the one teaching me when it comes to pronunciation and certain aspects of grammar. I do sometimes worry about the years to come. Will my French be strong enough to navigate the complexities of adolescence, for example. But it reassures me to watch my daughter slip effortlessly between English with her father and French with me. If her feelings become too complex to express in French, we can always pivot to the native language we share. This summer, our family moved to France for a one-year sabbatical, so we will be discovering a new culture in addition to our language learning. Whatever languages we use in the future, this opportunity to broaden our horizons together will always remain precious. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Meta's Muse AI agent is very powerful — but not enough to overcome my kids' annoying school apps
events.summary: The Meta Muse AI agent, which acts as a personal assistant of sorts. Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images I spent a week trying out Muse and gave it access to my email, credit cards, and even Apple health data. It was able to do some helpful tasks for me, like organizing my inbox, but failed at helping with school forms. Even though it failed fairly often, I imagine it will get better and more useful. I'm a convert! There are a whole slew of very good reasons that I should feel nervous about giving Meta access to my health data. Or my credit cards. Or read/write access to my personal and work emails and calendar. I think we can all reasonably agree that over the last 20 years, Meta has given reasonable people some very reasonable reasons to think that granting it that much access to personal, private data is very unreasonable. But I am not a reasonable person. Which is why I stopped worrying about AI killing us all and learned to love Muse , Meta's new AI agent. Well, mostly. Muse launched earlier this month and has received a surprisingly warm reaction. I guess I say surprising because Meta has struggled to launch an AI app that has caught on with consumers. Remember "Vibes," the video generating Sora competitor? Me neither. Muse's strength is that it's an easy-to-use and understand AI agent. You use it to send it to-do tasks like "organize my inbox" or "Find me a good travel stroller for my upcoming trip" instead of the more common things you use LLMs like ChatGPT for (such as text generation or in place of Google searching). Muse researches and offers to buy a travel stroller in this example from Meta's press release. Meta I started by testing it with some obvious, straightforward tasks. First, I asked it to look through my email and send me a daily digest of "important" emails (my inbox gets quickly clogged with PR pitches and newsletters). It did this admirably well. I also asked it to look at my credit and debit cards and tell me what subscription I could cancel — it suggested Flickr (for irrational reasons only understandable to my human soul, I'm keeping it). What more could I do? If I gave it more and more access to my life beyond my email and credit cards (!!) would it help me even more? I gave Muse two main buckets of tasks. 1. Be my kids' secretary School-age kids generate a tremendous amount of paperwork, form-filling-out, calendar balancing, and various online sign-ups and email, and keeping on top of it all feels impossible. An AI agent to help me sift through this would be far more useful than in my professional life. But could it cut through the weird mess of strange and clunky apps that schools and kid activities all use? The task: Plan a kid's birthday at a trampoline park. This involved getting pricing and availability from the venue, and sending invites. The result: Failure, but mostly human failure. Muse tried, but ultimately, there are too many decisions about this to be made by the birthday boy (and needed real phone calls to the venue), so this wasn't a good job to outsource to AI. (Since then, Meta has updated Muse to allow it to make calls, but I don't love the idea of subjecting a human to an AI call.) The task: Keep on top of my kids' school and activity notifications. Staying on top of things across a variety of apps and emails for school and activities is my personal nightmare — so send me a digest. The result: Mixed results. While it flagged items that came in via email, the school's Russian nesting dolls of information sometimes stymied Muse's ability to actually help me. For example, I needed to fill out a Google Form for band signup, and that Form lived inside a link from ParentSquare. But my ParentSquare login is via my Google account — and Muse's browser version of the site didn't include the Google login option. (I told a Meta PR person a few days later about my Google login issue. They conferred with the engineering team, and gave me steps to troubleshoot a way to log in. Success, although that kind of concierge service isn't available to most users.) It also couldn't track any of the Girl Scouts planning information, because that app happens in a busy WhatsApp group — and it couldn't view WhatsApp messages. I was mad at Muse when it couldn't checkout on the Girl Scouts' website. And yes, I named my agent "Mark." Business Insider / screenshot The task: Renew Girl Scouts annual membership. The result: The Girl Scouts of America defeat AI! The Girl Scouts' website has always been really frustrating to use, and although Muse almost could do it, it couldn't complete the final payment section without the site timing out. I ended up having to do it on my computer. 2. Personal health data I needed to go full Muse guinea pig and give it all the sensitive data I could think of. I connected it to my Apple health and fitness tracker data. Could Muse make me healthier? Here you go Muse, have my Apple Health data! Here you go Muse, have my Apple Health data! Business Insider / screenshot The task: Help me lower my resting heart rate. I'll be honest, I wasn't that interested in doing this but I wanted to give it something to do. The result: Sure, fine. It looked at my data and told me my resting heart rate was fine, but suggested I could improve it by sleeping better (no thanks). The task: Book my annual physical. I gave it my doctor's name and told it to book for November. The result: Failure. After giving it a bunch of info like my date of birth and last four digits of SSN (yikes), it couldn't get past updating the insurance info and told me to call the office. No way would I pay $11 in fees for same-day delivery of $9 cookies! Business Insider / screenshot The task: Order cookies from Walmart+ to arrive 2 days before my period each month. The result: Failure. The menstrual cycle data from Apple doesn't sync with Muse, and it won't connect to the other period tracker app on my phone. It was able to start a Walmart order, and I told Muse to only order with free shipping, but it took that too literally and didn't notice it was tacking on a bunch of extra same-day delivery fees. I told it to cancel the task and not place the order. My takeaway: Muse was helpful, but not ready to fix my life yet I can see the promise here — it was able to accomplish (or at least half-accomplish) some stuff that could be genuinely helpful. A colleague of mine used Muse to successfully dispute a health bill with his insurance. But it can't yet do the really annoying stuff I don't want to do myself. Meta acknowledged that Muse can't do everything (yet). "Some of that friction is intentional," said Jimmy Raimo, spokesperson for Meta told me. "If fees look high or a login looks off, Muse is designed to stop and check rather than push through. We'd rather it ask than get it wrong." Although the failures were disappointing, nothing was life-ruining. I just simply had to do the tasks myself on a computer. I'd rather it fail than accidentally spe

events.title: LSU coach Lane Kiffin was asking ChatGPT for legal advice, friend says
events.summary: During a critical moment, Lane Kiffin's friend said the LSU football coach turned to an unlikely source. Gus Stark/LSU/University Images via Getty Images LSU football coach Lane Kiffin's program was in the middle of an unprecedented legal fight. Sports attorney Tom Mars, Kiffin's friend, told ESPN that the LSU coach turned to ChatGPT. Mars said Kiffin would send him screenshots of ChatGPT's legal responses, which were wrong on the law. Indiana head coach and reigning national champion Curt Cignetti has Google in his corner. Apparently, LSU football coach Lane Kiffin relies on ChatGPT. According to Kiffin's friend, who is also one of the nation's most prominent sports lawyers, the LSU football coach turned to ChatGPT for legal advice at a critical moment for the university. "Usually, when I would express an opinion about what LSU was doing, Lane would reply with a screenshot from ChatGPT that supported LSU's position, which was almost always wrong," Attorney Tom Mars told ESPN. Despite incurring the wrath of rivals, the Southeastern Conference (SEC), the NCAA, and many, many talking heads, LSU initially fought to add former NFL players Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris to Kiffin's inaugural squad. In November, LSU announced that it had hired Kiffin away from the Ole Miss Rebels, a fellow SEC member, with a seven-year, $91 million deal that came in the middle of the Rebels' College Football Playoff run. Both Wright and Harris played under Kiffin at Ole Miss, and both signed with NFL teams after going undrafted. The situation escalated to the point that the SEC, of which LSU is a founding member, went to court to secure a ruling allowing conference leaders representing the other members to meet and consider LSU's status. If LSU were kicked out of the SEC, the university would likely lose out on lucrative conference TV rights payments. With university presidents, state attorneys general, governors, and even members of Congress involved, LSU was facing an unprecedented fight over its very future. Mars said that he told his friend the stakes were too high to rely on an AI chatbot. "Eventually I told him that a guy with a $91 million contract ought to have a top-notch lawyer on speed dial and not be using ChatGPT for legal advice," he said. Representatives for Kiffin, Mars, and OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. LSU declined to comment. While Wright and Harris prevailed in state court, LSU ultimately backed down and announced a final 2026 roster that did not include either player. Mars said Kiffin reached out to him, which means the LSU coach, known for not doing things by the book, followed OpenAI 's terms for this area. The ChatGPT maker, like its competitors, makes it clear that users should not rely on an AI chatbot as the sole source of professional advice. Specifically, it says ChatGPT is not "a substitute for professional advice." It remains an unsettled area of law what happens if a user follows the chatbot's advice and suffers harm. In a federal court case in Illinois, OpenAI has argued that ChatGPT is not a lawyer and does not practice law in response to a $10.3 million suit filed by a life insurance company. Nippon Life Insurance Company has argued that OpenAI is to blame for ChatGPT giving inaccurate legal advice to a former disability claimant who, relying on ChatGPT, breached a settlement agreement with the insurance company. As for Kiffin, Mars said it's unlikely the LSU coach will rely on ChatGPT for legal advice again. "Lane ignored most of my unsolicited advice, but I don't think he'll be using ChatGPT anymore for legal advice," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Student-debt relief is in limbo for borrowers pursuing a major forgiveness program for public servants
events.summary: Student-loan borrowers are facing delays getting relief through the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program. nirat/Getty Images Student-loan borrowers have reported delays with Public Service Loan Forgiveness processing. Some have made the required amount of payments, but are waiting for the relief to be reflected. At the same time, PSLF eligibility is facing ongoing litigation. A major student-loan forgiveness program is facing changes — and delays. Student-loan borrowers pursuing Public Service Loan Forgiveness, which forgives student debt for government and nonprofit workers after 10 years of qualifying payments, have found that their payment count er s have not updated to reflect payments that put them at the forgiveness threshold. For example, some borrowers who made their 120th payment over the past few months are still waiting for their payment counter on Federal Student Aid to reflect that they qualify for relief. The delay means borrowers must choose between continuing to make payments they might not owe or stopping payments and risking being flagged for delinquency. The Education Department did not comment on the delay or when it will be resolved, and a spokesperson said that the agency "remains committed to ensuring that every qualifying payment is properly credited to a borrower's account." The processing delays are not the only challenge borrowers pursuing PSLF face. President Donald Trump's student-loan repayment overhaul implemented stricter rules on determining a qualifying PSLF payment, and the Department of Education is fighting in court to implement its plan to narrow eligibility for the program. Some borrowers also had some of their PSLF payments rescinded , which the administration cited to code errors. Beyond PSLF, borrowers have been navigating Trump's overhaul and the higher bills it has brought. The administration has said that its changes are intended to simplify a complex repayment system and compel colleges to lower their tuition. Still, borrowers have reported administrative errors and inaccurate account statuses, putting their budgets in limbo. Ayelet Sheffey covers all things student debt, from the latest Education Department news to stories of borrowers navigating their loans. To stay up to date on her coverage, sign up to get email alerts for her new stories here . What's ahead for PSLF borrowers Following Trump's repayment changes, the stakes are higher for borrowers to be exactly on time with their payments. Prior to the changes, borrowers were given a 15-day grace period to make a payment so it would count toward PSLF progress. Now, a borrower must make a payment exactly on the day it is due; making a payment even one day late will not count toward PSLF. Federal Student Aid's guidance said that a payment qualifies if it is made "on or before the due date," and that payments don't need to be consecutive to qualify. This change applies to both the new income-driven Repayment Assistance Plan created under the overhaul, as well as existing repayment plans. Eligibility for the program is also in litigation. The administration planned to implement a rule on July 1 that would have narrowed PSLF eligibility, excluding employers that do not meet its definition of "public service." Courts blocked the rule following lawsuits filed by nonprofits. The Education Department appealed the ruling at the end of August, and the case will not progress through the DC Circuit. There are no immediate changes to PSLF while the court makes another determination. Have a story to share about student loans? Contact this reporter at asheffey@businessinsider.com .
